newsitem.title: UK: Gene found that makes hearts grow.
newsitem.headline: Gene found that makes hearts grow.

text.p: British researchers said on Tuesday they had found a gene that seems to help make the heart grow in response to strenuous physical exercise.
They said their finding could help doctors prevent heart attacks in people at risk of developing an enlarged heart.

Steve Humphries and colleagues at University College Hospital in London said their studies on army recruits showed the gene, a variant of a well-known gene called "ACE", seemed to control growth of human heart muscle.
The hearts of cadets who completed a strenuous 10-week training course and who had the ACE gene variant showed 25 percent more growth than cadets who had some other variant of the gene.
"This is an enormous difference in the growth of the heart compared to the men who did not have the variant gene," Hugh Montgomery, a cardiologist who worked on the study, said in a statement.

The results were so startling that some people doubted them. "It's caused a little difficulty getting this paper published because everbody looked at this and said 'no this can't be right'," he added in a telephone interview.
"These results are strangely powerful and we have to be sure they are correct."
But Montgomery said he was not entirely surprised.
The ACE gene controls an enzyme known as angiotensin-converting enzyme. ACE closes down the capillaries, keeping blood pressure up and making the heart work harder.
"Everybody's got two copies of this gene, but some seem to have this version that has a little extra," Montgomery said.
Those who have two copies of the extra gene Montgomery's tests show those who produce more ACE grow bigger hearts.
It still was not clear if this was a bad thing but it could be in some people, the researchers stressed.
"It is important to point out that the growth in the hearts of these young men was absolutely normal and appropriate for the amount of exercise they were undertaking," Montgomery said.

The recruits showed no real differences in their blood pressure, but it could be that, in those who had the extra heart growth, blood pressure shot up during exercise. Montgomery said this would be difficult to measure.

Where the gene could be important is in those who have high blood pressure -- about 23 percent of the population in Britain. One-quarter of people with high blood pressure develop an enlarged left ventricle of the heart, which increases the risk of heart attack and stroke.
Montgomery said more tests were already under way and the group hoped to report next year.
Drugs known as ACE inhibitors reduce the risk of abnormal heart growth and are widely used to treat high blood pressure.
Montgomery said the findings could increase the popularity of the drugs, which have milder side-effects than other blood pressure drugs.
The research, which was funded by the British Heart Foundation, was published in the journal Circulation.
